Ectopic parathyroid adenomas are seen in about a fifth of all cases of primary hyperparathyroidism, with 1–2% located within the mediastinum. Mediastinal parathyroid adenomas (MPAs) defined as an adenoma found below the clavicle, represent a rare but clinically significant cause of persistent or recurrent primary hyperparathyroidism. The first reported case of MPA and its successful resection was that of Charles Martell, a former captain in the United States Merchant Marines ( ). He underwent six unsuccessful cervical explorations before Dr Oliver Cope and Dr Edward Churchill resected a 3 cm tumour from the mediastinum ( ). MPAs result from aberrant embryologic migration of the inferior parathyroid glands along the thymic descent pathway, leading to their final position within the anterior or posterior mediastinum. The atypical location of MPAs poses considerable diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, often contributing to surgical failures in reoperative parathyroid disease ( , ). Advances in imaging and surgical techniques have altered outcomes of patients with MPA. The parathyroid glands in the mediastinum can be difficult to access due to the variable anatomy, and therefore accurate localization prior to surgery is essential. Conventional imaging techniques have limited sensitivity in localization of MPAs, and newer modalities such as four-dimensional computed tomography (4D-CT), hybrid single-photon emission computed tomography/computed tomography (SPECT/CT), and positron emission tomography (PET) using novel tracers such as 18 F-fluorocholine (FCH)—has significantly improved localization accuracy ( , ). Historically, surgical excision of MPAs required open thoracotomy or sternotomy, both associated with significant morbidity. However, minimally invasive thoracoscopic and robotic-assisted techniques have revolutionized access to deep mediastinal lesions, offering reduced operative trauma, shorter hospital stays, and improved patient outcomes. Emphasis is placed on the integration of modern imaging and minimally invasive techniques, as well as the unresolved controversies and future directions in optimizing outcomes for this uncommon but demanding clinical entity. By the 7th of gestation, the glands migrate caudally with the thyroid and thymus after losing their connection with the pharyngeal wall to rest in their conventional position ( ). The superior glands which originate from the fourth pharyngeal pouch migrate a shorter distance and attach to the posterior surface of the upper third of the thyroid gland. Most superior glands are constant in their position, with nearly 80% of them found to be within an area of 2 cm 2 at the intersection of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the inferior thyroid artery ( ). In comparison, the inferior parathyroid glands arise from the third pharyngeal pouch, which also gives rise to the thymus, are usually located on anterolateral surface of the lower pole of the thyroid gland or in the thymic tongue ( ). This longer course of migration caudally and medially along with the thymus primes the inferior parathyroid to be in ectopic positions than the superior parathyroid ( ). Aberrant migration or failure of separation of the inferior parathyroid from the thymic tissue can result in ectopic parathyroid tissue within the mediastinum ( , , ), or rarely in the aortopulmonary window ( ). Imaging modalities and localization Accurate localisation of MPAs remains a diagnostic challenge due to their size, position and overlap with other mediastinal structures. A central principle in evaluation is the use of multimodal imaging, as no single modality achieves ideal localisation. Combining anatomical and functional techniques enhances diagnostic accuracy, particularly in re-operative or complex cases. Ultrasound (US) US is widely used as the initial imaging modality for parathyroid localisation as it is readily available, non-invasive, and cost effective ( ). It provides excellent resolution for superficial cervical glands in expert hands. However, its utility is limited in mediastinal disease because of restricted acoustic penetration beyond the thoracic inlet ( ). Therefore, in mediastinal disease, US contributes primarily to the exclusion of cervical sources rather than the direct identification of mediastinal parathyroids. In previously failed parathyroid excisions, US-guided fine needle aspiration for parathyroid hormone (PTH) washout can be considered to substantiate US findings if a parathyroid adenoma candidate is identified ( , , ). However, one has to be cautious of the risk of FNA inducing parathyromatosis ( , ) and risk of seeding from parathyroid carcinoma ( , ). Technetium-99m sestamibi (MIBI) scintigraphy MIBI scintigraphy remains a standard first-line imaging modality for localizing hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue in primary hyperparathyroidism, with overall sensitivity ranging from 70% to 90% for typical cervical adenomas ( , ). However, its performance declines significantly in ectopic and mediastinal parathyroid disease ( ). Deep thoracic location, small gland size, multiglandular disease, low PTH levels, and coexistent thyroid pathology all contribute to reduced sensitivity and higher false-negative rates ( , ). Combination with SPECT has demonstrated improved sensitivity and specificity ( - ). A meta-analysis demonstrated that SPECT/CT improves the sensitivity of parathyroid adenoma detection to 86%, significantly outperforming planar imaging (70%) and SPECT alone (74%) for both cervical and mediastinal disease ( ). In MPAs, reported detection rates are as low as 30–50%, largely due to attenuation by overlying structures and poor spatial resolution at greater depths. While positive MIBI localization to a mediastinal focus can effectively guide surgical planning, negative or equivocal results are common and should prompt further evaluation with other imaging modalities. It offers superior spatial and anatomical resolution, allowing detailed delineation of deep-seated or ectopic mediastinal lesions. In one study, 4D-CT was found to be superior to sestamibi scan especially in reoperative settings or failed initial imaging or discordant preoperative US and sestamibi imaging ( - ). In another study, imaging with 4D-CT localized the adenomas in 85.7% and more so in multiglandular disease ( ). Several recent studies have reported higher sensitivity compared with sestamibi/SPECT, though at the expense of higher radiation exposure ( ). The decision to use 4D-CT should therefore balance diagnostic benefits against cumulative radiation dose. Selective venous sampling (SVS) or arteriography SVS of PTH or arteriography can be useful in patients with persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism and negative imaging. By measuring PTH gradients across venous territories draining the mediastinum, SVS can lateralise or localise the hyperfunctioning source. Although invasive, and hence not a primary imaging modality, SVS remains a valuable problem-solving tool, particularly in the re-operative setting or when surgical planning demands precise localisation ( , ). In the case of mediastinal adenomas, the thymic vein should be a primary target of venous sampling. In a study of 19 cases of proved mediastinal parathyroid glands, selective arteriography was positive in 10 of 15 cases (67%), but SVS only localized 8 of 15 cases (53%) ( ). Using SVS in their cohort of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism, Sun et al. showed a 100% sensitivity and positive predictive value for the mediastinal lesions ( ). A meta-analysis showed super-SVS to be more accurate than other parathyroid venous sampling methods ( ). It is important to note the potential pitfalls of venous sampling techniques. The thymic vein typically drains into the innominate vein but may instead drain into the internal mammary vein or into a common trunk with the inferior thyroid vein. In the latter cases, increased PTH levels may appear in the inferior thyroid vein despite the presence of a mediastinal adenoma, complicating differentiation between inferior parathyroid and mediastinal lesions. Additionally, the presence of thymic-thyroid connections can also results in elevated PTH levels in the thyroid veins, limiting ability to distinguish between cervical and mediastinal adenomas ( , ). When results are negative, discordant, or suggest an ectopic mediastinal source, 4D-CT or 18F-FCH PET/CT should be pursued for further localisation. SVS is reserved for patients where non-invasive modalities have failed to localise the lesion. Current guidelines from the American Association of Endocrine Surgeons emphasize that imaging selection should be tailored to the clinical context and available institutional expertise, with multimodal imaging offering the highest diagnostic yield for mediastinal and ectopic parathyroid disease ( ). However, the appearance of techniques such as VATS and robot-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (RATS) improved success rates, reduced morbidity, and shorter hospital stays compared to open procedures. Mediastinoscopy, though technically a transcervical approach, refers specifically to the anatomical plane anterior to the trachea and posterior to the great vessels. The first reports of successful transcervical mediastinoscopic excision of parathyroid adenomas located in thymus or upper mediastinum were in 1980s and 1990s ( , ). In a series of 4 patients with anterior mediastinal parathyroids who underwent previous cervicotomy, video-assisted mediastinoscopy (VAM) safely enabled resection of the parathyroids safely with a short hospital stay ( ). In another study mediastinoscopy was performed in 5 patients, with the lesions seen anterior to the trachea or carina ( ). However, the role of mediastinoscopy is limited in MPAs as only few lesions are seen in the pretracheal space ( ). VATS VATS has become the preferred minimally invasive approach for resection of deep MPAs, particularly those inaccessible through a cervical incision. Since the first successful VATS removal reported in the early 1990s, this technique has largely replaced traditional open sternotomy or thoracotomy for appropriately localized lesions ( ). Quite a few series have reported on the efficacy of VATS parathyroidectomy for MPAs ( - ). Most lesions in the anterior mediastinum are approached via the left side ( ). Advantages of VATS include reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stay, faster recovery, minimal scarring, and decreased risk of sternal wound complications compared with open approaches ( , - ). Intraoperative PTH monitoring confirms biochemical cure in real time. Reported cure rates exceed 95%, with very low recurrence and complication rates ( ). RATS RATS extends minimally invasive options—offering three-dimensional (3D) vision, wristed instruments, and fine dissection in deep mediastinal spaces making it particularly advantageous when lesions lie in constrained mediastinal niches. Case series and small comparative studies report reduced conversion rates, positive margins, and composite adverse outcomes compared to VATS, with similar or shorter length of stay and low morbidity ( , ). In a single centre study reported by Stuart et al. , 8 patients underwent RATS parathyroidectomy with a long operative time (178 minutes), shorter hospital stay of 2 days, with only 1 patient suffering a complication of chylothorax ( ). However, cost, operative time, and availability remain constraints for many centres globally. Methylene blue can be administered intravenously or selectively injected intra-arterially into the feeding vessel of a MPA, producing a direct blue discoloration that facilitates rapid visual identification ( , ). Practical surgical algorithm Surgical treatments should be addressed by experienced surgical teams involving endocrine and thoracic surgeons, in a facility where open/ endoscopic surgeries of the thorax are routinely undertaken. Ectopic parathyroid glands located in the superior mediastinum or near the aortic arch may be accessed via a cervical approach ( ). Minimally invasive techniques should be considered as first choice for MPAs that cannot be approached via the cervical approach. Open surgical techniques such as partial or full median sternotomy, anterior mediastinotomy, or thoracotomy may be required if minimally invasive options are not available and for deep or complex lesions in anatomically complex locations precluding safe surgery. Intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring (IOPTH) is recommended to confirm completion of resection ( , ). In patients who are not surgical candidates or refuse surgery, selective arterial embolization or medical management with calcimimetic may achieve biochemical remission ( - ). Summary of key challenges in management Embryological complexity and anatomical variability Aberrant migration of inferior parathyroids with the thymus explains why most ectopic glands are mediastinal. However, there is a wide distribution along the thymic descent pathway (anterior mediastinum, aortopulmonary window, pericardium, posterior mediastinum) making localisation unpredictable and increasing the difficulty in surgical planning. Diagnostic difficulties in localization Cervical US has limited utility in lesions below the thoracic inlet, and traditional sestamibi SPECT/CT has reduced sensitivity in intrathymic, cystic, or small lesions. While advanced modalities such as 4D-CT and 8F-fluorocholine PET/CT can improve the detection of MPAs, they also have increased radiation exposure and cost. Clinicians must balance radiation risk against the potentially higher diagnostic yield that prevents failed operations and re-exploration. Advanced imaging modalities might also not be accessible in resource-limited settings. Invasive SVS may be required in challenging reoperative cases. Surgical access and approach selection Lesions above the innominate vein may be retrieved trans-cervically, but deeper lesions often require thoracic access. Historically, sternotomy/thoracotomy ensured exposure but with significant morbidity. Minimally invasive techniques (VATS and RATS) achieve high cure rates with lower morbidity, yet demand advanced expertise, longer operative times, and specialised resources. Clinicians need to balance the trade-offs between exposure, safety, recovery time, costs and complication risks. Multidisciplinary coordination between endocrine surgery, thoracic surgery, radiology, nuclear medicine is essential but not uniformly available across centres. Conclusions MPAs continue to pose important diagnostic and therapeutic challenges because of embryological variability, atypical anatomical locations, and limits of conventional imaging. Advances in cross-sectional and molecular imaging (notably 4D-CT and 18 F-FCH PET/CT) and the wider adoption of minimally invasive thoracic techniques (VATS and RATS) have markedly improved the ability to localise and resect ectopic glands while reducing morbidity compared with open sternotomy. Nonetheless, persistent problems—discordant or negative imaging, multiglandular disease, radiation exposure, limited access to advanced imaging and surgical expertise, and the increased risks associated with reoperation—remain unresolved in many centres. Optimal management requires a pragmatic, stepwise imaging strategy that escalates to high-yield modalities when first-line tests are inconclusive, routine use of IOPTH to confirm biochemical cure, and selection of the least-invasive approach that reliably reaches the lesion. In complex, re-operative, or indeterminate cases, SVS and multidisciplinary collaboration (endocrinology, endocrine and thoracic surgery, nuclear medicine, radiology) are critical to reduce failed explorations and complications. Future efforts should prioritise equitable access to advanced imaging, prospective comparison of imaging and surgical approaches, and pathways that standardize care across centres to further improve patient outcomes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and 4D-MRI MRI provides excellent soft tissue contrast and avoids ionising radiation, making it suitable for patients in whom radiation exposure should be minimized ( ). Although uncommon as a primary modality, MRI is useful for mediastinal localization due to its soft tissue contrasting ability. When performed with dynamic contrast-enhanced protocols (4D-MRI), it can also depict enhancement kinetics like those used in 4D-CT by capitalising on the hypervascular nature of the parathyroid glands in comparison to surrounding lymph nodes ( ). A comparison with US and sestamibi shows that MRI can identify more adenomas and is also able to identify most ectopic lesions ( ). Some studies have shown similar accuracy in parathyroid detection using 4D-MRI and 4D-CT ( ). Selective venous sampling (SVS) or arteriography SVS of PTH or arteriography can be useful in patients with persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism and negative imaging. By measuring PTH gradients across venous territories draining the mediastinum, SVS can lateralise or localise the hyperfunctioning source. Although invasive, and hence not a primary imaging modality, SVS remains a valuable problem-solving tool, particularly in the re-operative setting or when surgical planning demands precise localisation ( , ). In the case of mediastinal adenomas, the thymic vein should be a primary target of venous sampling. In a study of 19 cases of proved mediastinal parathyroid glands, selective arteriography was positive in 10 of 15 cases (67%), but SVS only localized 8 of 15 cases (53%) ( ). Using SVS in their cohort of persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism, Sun et al. showed a 100% sensitivity and positive predictive value for the mediastinal lesions ( ). A meta-analysis showed super-SVS to be more accurate than other parathyroid venous sampling methods ( ). It is important to note the potential pitfalls of venous sampling techniques. The thymic vein typically drains into the innominate vein but may instead drain into the internal mammary vein or into a common trunk with the inferior thyroid vein. In the latter cases, increased PTH levels may appear in the inferior thyroid vein despite the presence of a mediastinal adenoma, complicating differentiation between inferior parathyroid and mediastinal lesions. Additionally, the presence of thymic-thyroid connections can also results in elevated PTH levels in the thyroid veins, limiting ability to distinguish between cervical and mediastinal adenomas ( , ). Practical imaging algorithm For most patients with primary hyperparathyroidism, US and sestamibi SPECT/CT remain the first-line imaging combination. When results are negative, discordant, or suggest an ectopic mediastinal source, 4D-CT or 18F-FCH PET/CT should be pursued for further localisation. SVS is reserved for patients where non-invasive modalities have failed to localise the lesion. Current guidelines from the American Association of Endocrine Surgeons emphasize that imaging selection should be tailored to the clinical context and available institutional expertise, with multimodal imaging offering the highest diagnostic yield for mediastinal and ectopic parathyroid disease ( ). Surgical options for MPAs The treatment option for a mediastinal parathyroid gland is centred on surgical resection. The choice of surgical approach depends on the precise anatomical location of the gland, as determined by preoperative localization studies mentioned earlier. Open approaches Most MPAs situated in the anterior mediastinum along the thymus can be approached via the standard cervical approach or inferior mobilisation with thymectomy. During such an approach attention should be taken to safeguard critical anatomical structures in the superior mediastinum such as the innominate vessels as they may tend to get pulled up and be prone for inadvertent injury. In one study of the 16 patients with mediastinal lesions approached via a transcervical approach, 7 patients required conversion to a partial sternotomy and 2 required a video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) ( ). Lesions deeper in the mediastinum required traditional surgical approaches such as sternotomy or thoracotomy but were associated with significant morbidity ( , , ). Traditional surgical approaches, such as median sternotomy and thoracotomy, have been the procedures of choice for MPAs that could not be approached by the cervical approach. However, the appearance of techniques such as VATS and robot-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (RATS) improved success rates, reduced morbidity, and shorter hospital stays compared to open procedures. Minimally invasive approaches Mediastinoscopy The technique was first introduced as a diagnostic approach for mediastinal pathology—has occasionally been adapted for the resection of parathyroid adenomas located in the superior or anterior mediastinum, particularly when lesions lie just below the thoracic inlet and are inaccessible via a standard cervical incision. Mediastinoscopy, though technically a transcervical approach, refers specifically to the anatomical plane anterior to the trachea and posterior to the great vessels. The first reports of successful transcervical mediastinoscopic excision of parathyroid adenomas located in thymus or upper mediastinum were in 1980s and 1990s ( , ). In a series of 4 patients with anterior mediastinal parathyroids who underwent previous cervicotomy, video-assisted mediastinoscopy (VAM) safely enabled resection of the parathyroids safely with a short hospital stay ( ). In another study mediastinoscopy was performed in 5 patients, with the lesions seen anterior to the trachea or carina ( ). However, the role of mediastinoscopy is limited in MPAs as only few lesions are seen in the pretracheal space ( ). VATS VATS has become the preferred minimally invasive approach for resection of deep MPAs, particularly those inaccessible through a cervical incision. Since the first successful VATS removal reported in the early 1990s, this technique has largely replaced traditional open sternotomy or thoracotomy for appropriately localized lesions ( ). Quite a few series have reported on the efficacy of VATS parathyroidectomy for MPAs ( - ). Most lesions in the anterior mediastinum are approached via the left side ( ). Advantages of VATS include reduced postoperative pain, shorter hospital stay, faster recovery, minimal scarring, and decreased risk of sternal wound complications compared with open approaches ( , - ). Intraoperative PTH monitoring confirms biochemical cure in real time. Reported cure rates exceed 95%, with very low recurrence and complication rates ( ). RATS RATS extends minimally invasive options—offering three-dimensional (3D) vision, wristed instruments, and fine dissection in deep mediastinal spaces making it particularly advantageous when lesions lie in constrained mediastinal niches. Case series and small comparative studies report reduced conversion rates, positive margins, and composite adverse outcomes compared to VATS, with similar or shorter length of stay and low morbidity ( , ). In a single centre study reported by Stuart et al. , 8 patients underwent RATS parathyroidectomy with a long operative time (178 minutes), shorter hospital stay of 2 days, with only 1 patient suffering a complication of chylothorax ( ). In a larger series of 17 patients including those with persistent disease and cervical explorations, who underwent parathyroidectomy RATS provided better visualization, ergonomics reduced physical demand of surgery, and safety ( ). However, cost, operative time, and availability remain constraints for many centres globally. Intraoperative marking techniques Intraoperative adjuncts are particularly valuable for mediastinal parathyroidectomy due to distorted anatomy, ectopic descent, or limited visualization by enhancing contrast between the adenoma and surrounding tissues to allow for localisation of MPA. Two commonly described techniques are methylene blue staining and indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging. Methylene blue can be administered intravenously or selectively injected intra-arterially into the feeding vessel of a MPA, producing a direct blue discoloration that facilitates rapid visual identification ( , ). Its advantages include immediate, robust staining of abnormal or enlarged glands and effectiveness in cases where standard preoperative localization is inconclusive. However, methylene blue carries notable limitations: neurotoxicity (especially in patients taking serotonergic agents), the risk of methemoglobinemia, and other systemic effects restrict its routine use ( ). Furthermore, normal parathyroid glands stain poorly, and evidence suggests that clinical outcomes are not significantly superior to operations performed without methylene blue ( , ), leading to ongoing debate about its role in modern practice and is generally reserved for select situations where other localization techniques are inadequate or unavailable. ICG fluorescence imaging involves intravenous administration of ICG followed by near-infrared (NIR) visualization, allowing well-perfused parathyroid tissue to fluoresce intraoperatively. Beyond localization, ICG provides dynamic assessment of gland perfusion and viability, helping surgeons decide whether a gland can be preserved or requires autotransplantation—an advantage particularly relevant in complex mediastinal dissections ( , ). Comparative studies and recent meta-analyses demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy, with pooled parathyroid identification sensitivity around 93.8% (95% CI: 90.0–96.2%) ( ), alongside associations with shorter operative times and lower rates of postoperative hypocalcemia due to improved viability assessment ( , ). Its disadvantages include the requirement for specialized NIR equipment, lack of standardized dosing and timing protocols, and reduced effectiveness in small or poorly perfused glands. Its disadvantages include the requirement for specialized NIR equipment, lack of standardized dosing and timing protocols, and reduced effectiveness in small or poorly perfused glands. Nevertheless, systemic adverse effects are rare, giving ICG a favorable overall safety profile. Practical surgical algorithm Surgical treatments should be addressed by experienced surgical teams involving endocrine and thoracic surgeons, in a facility where open/ endoscopic surgeries of the thorax are routinely undertaken. Ectopic parathyroid glands located in the superior mediastinum or near the aortic arch may be accessed via a cervical approach ( ). Minimally invasive techniques should be considered as first choice for MPAs that cannot be approached via the cervical approach. Open surgical techniques such as partial or full median sternotomy, anterior mediastinotomy, or thoracotomy may be required if minimally invasive options are not available and for deep or complex lesions in anatomically complex locations precluding safe surgery. Intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring (IOPTH) is recommended to confirm completion of resection ( , ). In patients who are not surgical candidates or refuse surgery, selective arterial embolization or medical management with calcimimetic may achieve biochemical remission ( - ). Summary of key challenges in management Embryological complexity and anatomical variability Aberrant migration of inferior parathyroids with the thymus explains why most ectopic glands are mediastinal. However, there is a wide distribution along the thymic descent pathway (anterior mediastinum, aortopulmonary window, pericardium, posterior mediastinum) making localisation unpredictable and increasing the difficulty in surgical planning. Diagnostic difficulties in localization Cervical US has limited utility in lesions below the thoracic inlet, and traditional sestamibi SPECT/CT has reduced sensitivity in intrathymic, cystic, or small lesions. While advanced modalities such as 4D-CT and 8F-fluorocholine PET/CT can improve the detection of MPAs, they also have increased radiation exposure and cost. Clinicians must balance radiation risk against the potentially higher diagnostic yield that prevents failed operations and re-exploration. Advanced imaging modalities might also not be accessible in resource-limited settings. Invasive SVS may be required in challenging reoperative cases. Surgical access and approach selection Lesions above the innominate vein may be retrieved trans-cervically, but deeper lesions often require thoracic access. Historically, sternotomy/thoracotomy ensured exposure but with significant morbidity. Minimally invasive techniques (VATS and RATS) achieve high cure rates with lower morbidity, yet demand advanced expertise, longer operative times, and specialised resources. Clinicians need to balance the trade-offs between exposure, safety, recovery time, costs and complication risks. Multidisciplinary coordination between endocrine surgery, thoracic surgery, radiology, nuclear medicine is essential but not uniformly available across centres. Conclusions MPAs continue to pose important diagnostic and therapeutic challenges because of embryological variability, atypical anatomical locations, and limits of conventional imaging. Advances in cross-sectional and molecular imaging (notably 4D-CT and 18 F-FCH PET/CT) and the wider adoption of minimally invasive thoracic techniques (VATS and RATS) have markedly improved the ability to localise and resect ectopic glands while reducing morbidity compared with open sternotomy. Nonetheless, persistent problems—discordant or negative imaging, multiglandular disease, radiation exposure, limited access to advanced imaging and surgical expertise, and the increased risks associated with reoperation—remain unresolved in many centres. Optimal management requires a pragmatic, stepwise imaging strategy that escalates to high-yield modalities when first-line tests are inconclusive, routine use of IOPTH to confirm biochemical cure, and selection of the least-invasive approach that reliably reaches the lesion. In complex, re-operative, or indeterminate cases, SVS and multidisciplinary collaboration (endocrinology, endocrine and thoracic surgery, nuclear medicine, radiology) are critical to reduce failed explorations and complications. Future efforts should prioritise equitable access to advanced imaging, prospective comparison of imaging and surgical approaches, and pathways that standardize care across centres to further improve patient outcomes.
